summary: Gives guidelines for using EPP's extension mechanisms to add new features and new object types. EPP is an XML protocol with a generic framework, so careful extension keeps it consistent. It is informational advice for those writing extensions.

plainLanguage.summary: If you add new rooms to a house, you should follow the building plan. This explains how to add new things to the registry language without breaking it.

questions: when to create a new object mapping
subtitle: Guidelines for designing and documenting extensions to EPP

tldr.problem: The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) is a generic XML-based framework for managing objects in a shared repository, and it needs to support extensions without breaking backward compatibility.
tldr.mechanism: EPP uses XML namespaces and wildcard elements to allow three levels of extension: command-response extensions to existing objects, object-level extensions for new managed types, and protocol-level extensions for new operational structures.
tldr.outcome: This gives protocol designers a systematic way to add features to EPP while preserving the core protocol, keeping extensions loosely coupled and preventing version conflicts.

today: RFC 3735 is an Internet Standard and remains the authoritative guide for extending EPP.

sections.title: Introduction to EPP Extensibility
sections.content:
The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) was originally designed as a standard for domain name registration between registrars and registries, but its architecture deliberately supports use in other provisioning scenarios. The protocol is built on XML and XML namespaces, and includes multiple extension mechanisms from the start.

EPP separates core protocol functions from object management logic, meaning that specific objects (like domain names) are defined as loosely coupled extensions to the base protocol. This design lets new features be added without changing the core protocol itself.
sections.plainLanguage: EPP is a toolkit for managing things in a database. It's built to let you add new tools without redesigning the whole toolkit.

sections.title: Principles of Protocol Extension
sections.content:
An extension to EPP adds features without altering the existing protocol schema. Extensions must be specified in XML, so any parser that understands EPP can also handle extensions. Designers must remember that extensions themselves may be extensible, creating a chain of increasingly specific functionality.

EPP extensions use XML namespaces identified by a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) to avoid conflicts. The URI both identifies the extension and serves as the namespace that contains it. Standards-track extensions use URN-based URIs following RFC 3688 registration procedures, while other extensions follow RFC 2396 URI syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: Extensions use unique names (URIs) so the protocol knows which new feature you are using. Each extension can itself have sub-extensions, like a family tree.

sections.title: Three Levels of Extension
sections.content:
EPP defines three extension mechanisms in order of increasing complexity. Command-response extension adds elements to an existing object mapping, such as adding new fields to a domain query. Object-level extension defines a new managed object type with the existing EPP command and response structures. Protocol-level extension defines entirely new protocol commands or structures.

A server announces available extensions in its greeting element as a list of svcExtension blocks containing URIs. A client requesting a session sends a login command specifying which extensions it wants to use. The server may restrict a client's access based on identity and authorization.
sections.plainLanguage: You can add a new field to an existing thing, define a brand new kind of thing to manage, or add completely new commands to the protocol.

sections.title: Documenting and Selecting Extensions
sections.content:
Extension designers should document their work with a suggested outline from the EPP core specification. Standards-track extensions of broad interest may be published as RFCs (Proposed Standard or Informational). Extensions for limited audiences or closed environments can be documented in formats suited to their intended users.

When choosing an extension form, designers should follow a decision tree: first check if the task can be solved by extending an existing object mapping; if not, consider creating a new object type; only if both are insufficient, design new protocol-level structures. This approach minimizes complexity. Designers should consult existing mapping archives, including the IETF, IANA, OASIS and XML.org registries.
sections.plainLanguage: Before building something new, see if you can reuse what already exists. Keep adding one small thing at a time rather than redesigning everything.

sections.title: Security and Internationalization
sections.content:
EPP extensions inherit the security services of the protocol structure being extended. Extensions may specify additional security services such as authentication, confidentiality, data integrity, authorization, access control or non-repudiation. Critically, extensions MUST NOT remove security services available in the underlying protocol.

Extensions must follow the same internationalization rules as EPP itself, observing the Internationalization Considerations in the EPP core specification and RFC 2277. EPP is represented in XML, which requires parsers to recognize UTF-8 and UTF-16, with support for other character encodings possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Extensions should keep the security that EPP already has, and they can add more. They must work with all the world's languages and writing systems.
